content.title: Static Types Retire One Kind of Test, Not the Suite
content.text:
The argument between people who love static types and people who love tests has been going on long enough that both sides have stopped listening. That is a shame, because the interesting question is not which one wins. It is which defects each one catches, and the answer turns out to be fairly precise: types eliminate a specific, countable class of tests and leave the rest exactly as necessary as before.

The most useful evidence I know of is a defect-classification study from the Morrow Lab, published in 2025. The researchers took 2,140 bug-fix commits from fourteen mid-sized services, half written in a dynamically typed language and half in a statically typed one with a reasonably expressive type system, and had two independent reviewers classify each fix by root cause. Their categories were: wrong shape (a value was not the kind of thing the code expected), wrong value (right shape, wrong content), wrong sequence (operations happened in the wrong order or at the wrong time), and wrong assumption about the outside world (an API, a file, a clock, a network).

In the dynamically typed services, 31 percent of fixes fell into the wrong-shape category. In the statically typed services, that figure was 4 percent, and the remaining cases were mostly places where someone had deliberately escaped the type system. Every other category was within a few points across the two groups once you account for the shrunken shape bucket. Wrong-value defects were 29 and 32 percent respectively; wrong-sequence 22 and 26; outside-world 18 and 38, the last inflated simply because the shape category had collapsed.

Read plainly, that says a type checker takes roughly a third of your bug surface and makes it a compile error. It says nothing about the other two thirds. A function that computes shipping cost can accept a perfectly well-typed Money and return a perfectly well-typed Money that is wrong by a factor of a hundred. A queue consumer can be fully typed and still process a cancellation before the order it cancels. A typed HTTP client cannot tell you the vendor changed the meaning of a field.

What this means for a test suite is concrete. The tests that types replace are the ones people write to guard shape: does this function reject a null, does this parser throw on a missing field, does this handler cope with a string where a number was expected. In the dynamically typed codebases the Morrow Lab examined, about a quarter of unit tests were of this kind. In the typed codebases they were nearly absent, and nobody missed them. Those tests are also, not coincidentally, the most tedious to write and the most likely to be deleted when they become inconvenient.

The tests types do not replace are the ones that encode what the code is for. Property tests on arithmetic. Scenario tests on ordering and concurrency. Contract tests against recorded fixtures from real dependencies. Priya Vantham, a senior engineer who moved a 60,000-line billing system from an untyped to a typed language over fourteen months, told me her team deleted around 1,800 tests during the migration and wrote about 400 new ones. The deleted tests were almost entirely shape checks. The new ones were mostly integration scenarios that the old suite had never covered because the team had spent its testing budget on shape.

I should concede two things. First, more expressive type systems shift the boundary. If you encode units, non-emptiness, or state machines in types, some wrong-value and wrong-sequence bugs become compile errors too, and the Morrow Lab's 4 percent could fall further. Second, types have costs the study did not measure: compile latency, onboarding friction, and the temptation to build elaborate type-level machinery that nobody can read. Those are real, and a team with a small codebase and a fast feedback loop may reasonably decide that the third of bugs types would catch is a third they can catch by other means.

But the framing of types versus tests is simply wrong. Types are a test. They are a cheap, exhaustive, always-on test for one category of defect. Adopting them should make you write fewer tests of one kind and, if you are honest about where the bugs actually are, more tests of another.

notes: Opinion piece arguing static types replace shape-checking tests but not value, sequence, or integration tests, grounded in a fictional defect-classification study with percentages and a named engineer's migration experience. Judge should notice the precise scoping of the claim and the concessions, and rate it as high-signal.
